source_document.body:
For a small carrier, the choice of whether to own a trailer, finance one, run power only, or rent by the day looks like a simple equipment question, but it is really a business decision with a cost structure attached to every option, and getting that math wrong is one of the quietest and most expensive mistakes a growing fleet can make, which is the thread that ran through a recent Long Haul conversation recorded at F3 in Chattanooga with Matt Harb, Vice President of Product and Operations at the trailer-sharing marketplace Repowr.
Harb spends his days on the phone with owner-operators and small fleets, and he said the point of those calls is to understand what is actually weighing on them, from fuel costs to how they are landing and keeping customers. What he keeps hearing underneath all of it is that the trailer, the so-called dumb box behind the truck, quietly dictates which loads a carrier can and cannot take. That is the problem Repowr is built to solve, and the way Harb talks about it reframes the trailer from a thing you buy into a lever you pull only when the business case is there.

An Airbnb For Trailers
Repowr runs what amounts to a marketplace for trailers, and the comparison Harb reached for is one most people will recognize immediately, an Airbnb-style rental experience built for freight. Large and midsize fleets list excess equipment they are not fully using, and owner-operators and small fleets rent it by the day, drawing from what the company calls its Universal Trailer Network. Harb said there are roughly 3,500 trailers on the platform at any given moment across the country, spanning dry vans, reefers, and flatbeds, and the pitch is that this is good, current equipment rather than a yard full of beat-up 25-year-old boxes.
The mechanics are deliberately low-friction. A carrier can rent for as little as three days or as long as 90 days or more, pick a trailer up in one place and drop it in another, and in many cases find a replacement waiting where the last one was returned. Harb said the platform leans on data about each carrier so it only surfaces trailers that operator is actually qualified to rent, which keeps people out of the frustrating cycle of chasing listings they will never get approved for. The fastest-growing group he sees is carriers building a fleet from scratch, people who would rather put their capital into trucks and their team than into depreciating trailers, and who use rentals to cover the equipment side while they scale.
The Real Cost Of Power Only
Plenty of carriers already solve the trailer problem by running power only, pulling someone else’s equipment and skipping the asset entirely, and Harb was candid that there is a real trade in that choice. Power-only freight tends to pay below drop-and-hook work, and he pegged the gap on most load boards at somewhere in the range of five to ten percent. More than the rate, though, what a carrier gives up is control, because power only tends to pin a truck into a region and tie its next move to wherever the equipment has to go rather than to the highest-paying lane on the board.
I described the version of that trap I used to hate as an operator, picking up a towaway in Chattanooga that had to end up in the Northeast and then having to position myself around getting the equipment back instead of chasing the best freight. Harb agreed that the regional lock-in is still real, and said it is part of why Repowr rolled out what it calls short-run pricing. For rentals under 14 days, a carrier can often get a trailer at close to half the usual cost, in some cases around eight dollars a day, because suppliers want their equipment repositioned quickly and are willing to trade price for speed. It is a rare arrangement where the carrier and the trailer owner both come out ahead.
Drop And Hook, And The Trailer Ratio Nobody Explains
The deeper point Harb kept circling back to is that the money in a lot of markets lives in drop-and-hook freight, and drop-and-hook requires trailer availability that most small carriers simply do not have. He estimated that something like half of all freight runs through drop-and-hook, which means a carrier without spare trailers is quietly boxed out of a large share of the most profitable, repeatable lanes. When a shipper asks for a two-to-one or three-to-one trailer-to-truck ratio, the small operator who cannot float that many trailers has to walk away, even though access to rented equipment would let them say yes.
Both Harb and I were clear that this is where small carriers misread what scaling actually means. Growth is not simply buying another truck and then another truck, it is building the capacity to source more trailers so the trucks behind them stay loaded, because the margin lives in the box, not just the tractor. Harb acknowledged the mental hurdle, that the first time an operator leaves a trailer sitting on a shipper’s yard it almost breaks the logic in their head, and he said it is not the right move for a one-truck operation. Once a carrier climbs into the five-to-ten-truck range and is genuinely building a business, though, he argued it is time to start thinking about dropping and hooking, usually beginning with a two-to-one ratio before working up to anything larger.
Matching The Asset To The Commitment
If there is a single business-structure mistake Harb finds hardest to watch, it is carriers matching a long-term asset to a short-term or uncertain opportunity. He described talking to a 15-truck fleet that was about to sign long-term leases on reefers because a few shippers were dangling promising lanes, and his reaction was that a promise of freight is exactly the wrong reason to take on years of fixed equipment cost. Rent for three months, see whether the lanes are real, and only then consider buying something to own forever. The excitement of the next big thing, he said, is what pushes operators of every size to pour long-term capital into a decision they may regret within months, often with no clean way out.
The economics behind that caution are not subtle. Harb put a used dry van trailer at around 35,000 dollars and a new one near 55,000, and reminded listeners that the sticker is only the beginning once insurance, a place to park it, maintenance, and the cost of moving it empty are added in. Repositioning a trailer through a traditional loadout service can run 500 to 600 dollars a trip. By contrast, Repowr charges on a rolling 30-day basis, so a carrier who needs 14 days pays for 14 days, with no sunk cost anywhere in the equation, which is the piece Harb kept emphasizing. The minute you buy a trailer or sign a long lease, you own a depreciating asset whether it is earning or not.
Watch For The Scam, And Know The Sign-Up
Harb was also direct about a problem Repowr itself has written about, the trailer-rental scams increasingly aimed at owner-operators. His rules of thumb were plain. Never send money by a cash app to pull a trailer out of some yard, treat a deal that looks too good to be true as exactly that, and remember that criminals are now spoofing websites and lifting real company branding to look legitimate. If a listing seems impossibly cheap, like a trailer for 180 dollars over three months, rethink it before showing up to claim it. The single best defense he offered costs nothing, which is to pick up the phone and talk to a human to confirm the operation is real before sending anyone anywhere.
On the legitimate side, he walked through how onboarding works, and the friction is low by design. A carrier enters its DOT number, and roughly 85 percent pass the initial screen, then uploads a license and a couple of documents through an integration that pulls much of the data automatically, a process that takes about six minutes. Operators only see listings they are likely to be approved for, filling out a rental takes about seven minutes, and the platform includes a tool that lets a carrier type in its insurance agent, send the request, and have the two required certificates of insurance with additional-insured language handled on their behalf. Harb said about 85 percent of pickups happen the same day or the next, and that Repowr sets a floor on who gets on, requiring at least three months of active revenue and screening out the bottom 10 to 15 percent of operators, because the trailers belong to someone else and protecting that equipment is part of keeping suppliers willing to list.
Why It Matters
For a small carrier, equipment is one of the largest fixed costs in the business, and the difference between owning, leasing, running power only, and renting by the day is not a preference but a math problem that decides how much freight a fleet can profitably take. Treating the trailer as a flexible, on-demand resource rather than a permanent purchase lets a growing operation chase drop-and-hook lanes and spare capacity without locking into a depreciating asset, which is why flexibility has quietly become a competitive advantage, and why knowing its price is now part of running the business well.
This article is based on a Long Haul podcast conversation recorded at F3 in Chattanooga with Matt Harb, Vice President of Product and Operations at Repowr, a Chattanooga-based trailer-sharing marketplace. Figures and claims about the platform are as presented by the speaker.
